title: Stocks vs bonds: owner or lender?
summary: See the one difference between a stock and a bond, and what it means for how each pays you.
objective: Tell a stock from a bond by asking whether you own part of the issuer or lent it money, and predict how each behaves when things go badly.

hook.prompt: You pay $1,000 for a company's bond. What have you just done?

options.text: Bought a small piece of the company
options.feedback: That's what buying its stock does. A bond works differently.

options.text: Paid a fee to join its investor club
options.feedback: Your $1,000 isn't a fee: you expect to get it back.

hook.explanation: A bond is an IOU. The company borrows your money and owes it back, which changes everything about how you get paid.

bricks.title: Owner or lender
bricks.body: A **stock** (also called a share) is a small piece of ownership in a company. Buy one and you're a part-owner. A **bond** is a loan. Buy one and you've lent money to a company or a government, which promises to pay you interest and return your money on a set date.

term.definition: A loan you make to a company or government, repaid with interest by a set date.

visual.alt: Two cards: Stock, where you own a slice of the company, and Bond, where you lend money and get interest plus your money back.
visual.html:

You're an owner

bricks.prompt: Maya pays a city $500. The city promises her 4% interest a year and her $500 back in 10 years. What did Maya buy?

options.feedback: A stock is a piece of ownership. Maya owns nothing here: she lent money and is promised it back.

options.text: Both: she owns part of the city and earns interest
options.feedback: Interest plus a set repayment date means a loan, not ownership. Lenders don't own what they lend to.

bricks.hint: Is Maya promised her money back on a set date?
bricks.explanation: Maya lent the city money in return for interest and repayment in 10 years. That's a bond, and governments issue them too.

bricks.title: How each one pays you
bricks.body: Because a lender is owed money, a bond pays its set **interest** whatever the profits, then returns your money. An owner is owed nothing. A stock pays off only if the company does well: its share price rises, or it shares profits as a **dividend**. If the company fails, lenders are paid back before owners. So bonds are usually steadier, while stocks can gain or lose much more.

term.definition: A share of a company's profits paid to its owners. The company can cut it at any time.

visual.alt: A table comparing stocks and bonds: what you are, what you get, who is paid first if the company fails, and how much the value swings.
visual.html:

bricks.prompt: A company has a terrible year and makes no profit. Who can still expect their regular payment?

options.text: Priya, who holds the company's bonds
Sam, who holds the company's stock
options.feedback: Owners share in profits, and there are none. Sam's dividend isn't promised, so it can be cut.

options.text: Neither: no profit means nobody gets paid
options.feedback: Bond interest is a debt the company owes whatever its profits. Only the owners' payments depend on profit.

bricks.hint: Which of them is owed money?
bricks.explanation: Priya is a lender, so her interest is owed even in a bad year. Sam is an owner, and owners share only in profits.

bricks.prompt: A company goes bust and sells everything it has. Who is first in line for that money?

options.text: Its shareholders, because they own the company
options.feedback: Owning it puts them last: lenders are paid back before owners, and often nothing is left for the owners.

options.text: Whoever put in the most money
options.feedback: The order depends on being a lender or an owner, not on how much each person put in.

bricks.hint: Think about who is owed money and who just owns a slice.
bricks.explanation: Bondholders lent the company money, so their claim comes first. Shareholders get only what's left, which is often nothing.

challenge.prompt: TechCo has a bad year: profits drop to zero and its share price falls 40%. Jo owns TechCo stock. Kim owns a TechCo bond. What most likely happens to them?

options.text: Jo's investment loses value, while Kim keeps getting her interest

options.feedback: The share price is what Jo's slice is worth. Kim is a lender, so she's owed her set interest and her money back.

options.text: Kim loses more, because lenders are paid last
options.feedback: It's the other way round: lenders are paid before owners.

options.text: Nothing changes for either of them
options.feedback: Jo's slice is worth 40% less, and with no profits her dividend could be cut too.

challenge.hint: Ask which of them is an owner and which is a lender.
challenge.explanation: Jo owns a slice, so she shares the drop. Kim lent money, so TechCo still owes her interest, unless it fails completely.

takeaways: A stock makes you a part-owner of a company; a bond makes you a lender to a company or government.
A bond promises set interest and your money back on a date; a stock promises nothing but can grow with the company.
If a company fails, bondholders are paid before shareholders, which is why bonds are usually the steadier of the two.
